Have you tried to enrich the local soil through permaculture? First off, if there's some monoculture, like some lawn grass growing on it, dig that garbage up right now and turn it into mulch (unless its a native variety then leave it, but create some patches in it so other native plants can grow). Also it goes without saying, but stop using (((weed killer)))) if you are. There's no such thing as 'weeds', thats a lie sold to promote artificial monoculture.

Is the soil too dry, despite regular watering/ rain? Create some shade to partially block the sun, and plant some hardy native scrubs or shrubs to help retain moisture. Is it barren/ infertile? Add compost and mulch to the soil to help fertilize it. Don't buy commercial fertilizer, compost and mulch is the natural way. You're recreating the natural cycle of growth, decay, and decomposition, and regrowth. This will assist with soil depth a bit as well, depending on how much you add.

Speaking of, for soil depth, let the native plants seed the soil and grow. Don't mess with it, just leave it be. Only remove something if it's noxious, like poison ivy. Over a couple years (this is a slow process), the plant roots will break up the rock, clay or w.e. is beneath the soil, and the cycle of growth & decay will build up organic matter, creating more top soil.

At any time during this process, you can introduce some crops you want to grow if you think they'll survive depending on the quality the soil has reached. Prefered the crops are native, but they don't have to be. Some rules though:

  • Don't plant a whole bunch of them, this is not monoculture. If the crop is native, you can get away with planting a bit more.

  • Spread the crops out, don't plant them right next to each other.

  • Don't plant them in a pattern, its not natural and will disrupt the permaculture.

  • clear as little soil as neccessary to plant the crops, preferably not at all. The less you disturb the permaculture the better.
It's aesthetic, but artificial. Instead of segregated monoculture, which requires constant maintenance, fertilizing, and watering, try for permaculture instead.
